data.title: Middle East Eye: Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner
data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner
Submitted by
Oscar Rickett
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 07:00
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali was extradited from Serbia and has been in Bahrain's Jau Prison since 2022
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali has been held in Jau Prison since he was deported from Serbia in January 2022 (ADHRB)
Off
The Council of Europe has called on Serbia to implement a European Court of Human Rights judgement, which held that the Balkan country had violated the European Convention on Human Rights when it extradited a Bahraini activist seeking asylum.
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali travelled to Serbia to seek asylum in November 2021 but was arrested by authorities there based on an Interpol red notice, which Ali’s lawyers say was unlawfully issued.
The European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure in January 2022 calling on Serbian authorities to refrain from extraditing Ali pending more information and particularly given the risk of torture or ill-treatment if he was returned.
Three days later, campaigners say a private plane, chartered by United Arab Emirates-based Royal Jet Airlines, took Ali to Bahrain.
Ever since then the activist, who fled Bahrain in 2011 and then lived in Iran before travelling to Serbia, has been held in Bahrain’s Jau Prison on two life sentences.
Inside the prison, Ali says he has been beaten, denied medical treatment, had his faith insulted and held in solitary confinement.
According to a recent call with fellow activists, a transcript of which was seen by Middle East Eye, Ali is currently being held in the prison’s Building Two, which houses violent offenders and those on serious drug charges.
Inside the building, the activist says these prisoners - acting on instruction from prison guards - beat and abuse him, creating a climate of fear that never lifts.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Rubio says Iran would 'blackmail the world' if it had a nuclear weapon
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Rubio says Iran would 'blackmail the world' if it had a nuclear weapon
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that if Iran had a nuclear weapon, it would use it to "blackmail the world and to kill people".
"It would control the straits, charge a toll, and decide who got energy and who did not," Rubio said during an interview with Fox News, and added that this could present an "unacceptable risk".
He also accused Tehran of using money received through sanctions relief or economic selling to build weapons and "export the revolution" rather than to "improve the lives of the Iranian people".
"They use the money to fund Hezbollah, they use the money to fund Hamas, they use the money to fund Shia militias in Iraq… they use the money to sponsor terrorism and assassination plots," Rubio said.
The US Secretary of State also criticised the country's leadership, saying: "Who calls the shots in Iran are radical Shia clerics with an apocalyptic vision of the future. They believe that it is a religious calling to trigger about the last days of the world, the apocalypse."

data.title: Middle East Eye: Araghchi adamant 'no change' in Iran's position, says conditions 'completely fair and reasonable'
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Araghchi adamant 'no change' in Iran's position, says conditions 'completely fair and reasonable'
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran's conditions to the US are "completely fair and reasonable", adding that there has been no change in the country's position.
"There have been claims made for several hours now, and I can state with certainty that there has been no change in Iran's position," Araghchi told Iranian media.
He said that Tehran's conditions for the deal are "clear", including it stance on the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"Right now, it's just the issue of the Strait of Hormuz. The opening of the Strait of Hormuz is also subject to the fulfillment of the conditions that we announced to the other side," Araghchi said.
"There are conditions from the Supreme Leader, and these conditions must be implemented in order for the Strait of Hormuz to open, and our mission was to convey these conditions to both the American side and all other countries and the international community, so that they are aware that Iran has a plan in this regard.
"Iran's conditions are completely fair and reasonable, and if the Americans claim that they are seeking an agreement or a peaceful solution, we should introduce this solution."

data.title: Middle East Eye: Araghchi tells UN's Guterres that Iran will 'never stop demanding justice'
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Araghchi tells UN's Guterres that Iran will 'never stop demanding justice'
Iran's foreign minister told UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres that Tehran will "never stop demanding justice" against orchestrators of "war crimes", making reference to US and Israel.
Abbas Araghchi stressed to Guterres that Iran will continue to defend its national sovereignty and territorial integrity, adding that "the Iranian nation will never stop demanding justice and holding accountable and punishing the perpetrators and perpetrators of the US and Zionist war crimes".
"Iran has always been steadfast in using diplomatic tools to protect its national interests and ensure peace in the region, but the United States has repeatedly betrayed diplomacy over the past decade and, by breaking its promise, has caused insecurity in the region," he said.
The Iranian foreign minister also highlighted what he described as Israel's "genocide and war-mongering" in Palestine, Lebanon, Syria and other countries.
Araghchi pointed to these violations as a reminder to the UN and the Security Council of the "responsibility to end Israel's impunity and stop the crimes committed in Gaza and the West Bank".

“I believe in the right to peaceful protest, I think that is important,” Miliband said in an interview on LBC on Tuesday.
Notably the foreign secretary avoided defending the ban on Palestine Action, which was introduced in the summer of 2025 under Keir Starmer’s premiership.
“On the specific issue of Palestine Action,” Miliband said, “there’s a case coming before the Supreme Court and so I’ll let that case play out, because I think it’s important that that court process takes its course.”
Pressed by interviewer Andrew Marr on whether he believed proscribing Palestine Action with “all those elderly people and vicars and grannies and so on" was politically sensible, Miliband responded: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised, but obviously the Supreme Court has got to look at this issue, and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as government.”

Large groups of attackers set fire to the Toubasi family’s homes in Jalud, forcing them to flee after earlier attacks aimed at taking over the property
A Palestinian man inspects a vehicle damaged in an Israeli settlers attack, in Al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, 29 September (Reuters/Mohamad Torokman)
Off
Dozens of Israeli settlers rampaged through villages in the occupied West Bank overnight into Tuesday, attacking Palestinians and setting fire to homes and cars.
Around 100 settlers raided Jalud, south of Nablus, shortly after midnight on Monday, targeting the homes of the Toubasi family.
The family had been forced out of their home in July following repeated settler attacks aimed at taking over the property.
They returned to the house hours before Tuesday’s attack after an Israeli court ordered the army to secure their return.
Settlers then arrived in large numbers and set fire to two homes belonging to the Toubasi family, forcing them to flee again.
Mahmoud Toubasi, the owner of one of the houses, said the family was shocked by the extent of the destruction and vandalism when they returned.
The fire destroyed the house, damaged its contents and left it uninhabitable, he said.

Army officials said “rioters” had blocked roads, set tyres on fire and thrown stones at troops, injuring three officers.

data.author: MEE staff

on

The visit follows reports that bin Zayed warned Netanyahu of a Hamas operation before 7 October
Emirati President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al-Nahyan in Berlin on 10 September 2026 (Ralf Hirschberger/AFP)
Off
The UAE has officially acknowledged hosting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for talks with President Mohammed bin Zayed on Sunday, its first such acknowledgement since establishing relations with Israel in 2020.
In a statement late on Monday, the Emirates News Agency said simply that bin Zayed "discussed with the Israeli prime minister the bilateral relations between the two countries and ways to strengthen and develop them".
The UAE released no official photograph of Sunday’s meeting. Its statement made no mention of the regional wars in which the UAE and Israel are involved - in occupied Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and Sudan.
Sources in the UAE told Haaretz that bin Zayed greeted Netanyahu at the airport.
The meeting also made the front pages of the UAE’s state-owned Al-Bayan and Al-Ittihad newspapers, which simply reprinted the official statement.
In May, Netanyahu’s office blindsided the UAE by revealing that he had secretly visited the country at the height of the Israeli-US war on Iran.
The Emirati foreign ministry responded by saying its relations with Israel "are public" and "not based on non-transparent or unofficial arrangements".
"Any claims regarding unannounced visits or undisclosed arrangements are entirely unfounded unless officially announced by the relevant authorities in the UAE," the statement said.
'Moral support'
The latest meeting follows a Haaretz report earlier this month that bin Zayed had given Netanyahu advance warning of a Hamas attack before 7 October 2023.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan
data.author: Ragip Soylu
data.summary:
Turkey’s $17bn fund scandal becomes a political crisis for Erdogan
Submitted by
Ragip Soylu
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 10:22
President vows accountability as the liquidation of 130 investment funds exposes ties to Turkey’s ruling elite
A picture taken in Istanbul shows US dollar banknotes and Turkish lira banknotes, 27 January 2021 (Ozan Kose/AFP)
Off
A crisis involving Turkish investment funds accused of running Ponzi-like schemes has affected half a million people, with authorities ordering the liquidation of some 130 funds worth $17bn earlier this month.
Already historic in scale, the financial turmoil has quickly become a major political crisis for President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s administration, exposing a web of connections between the funds, their managers and the ruling elite.
The most prominent political casualty so far has been Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a deputy head of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and family minister from 2016 to 2018. She resigned on Sunday after the opposition accused her of making substantial profits from share sales shortly before the funds crisis triggered a major stock market sell-off on 16 September.
Erdogan addressed the controversy on Monday, pledging to pursue those responsible for market manipulation and fraudulent trading schemes.
“Whoever lays a hand on the nation's rights, assets or legal interests will face us and the state,” he said.
The funds in question concentrated their holdings in illiquid stocks with low free floats, making their prices easier to inflate because relatively few shares were available for trading. For example, the Tera investment fund generated a return of over 1,500 percent over the past year, a figure that is totally illogical by any market calculation or method.

The Campaign Against Arms Trade, Action on Armed Violence, Shadow World Investigations UK and the Yemen Relief and Reconstruction Foundation signed the letter alongside academics and specialists in international relations, human rights and international law.
The signatories highlighted longstanding British support for Saudi military action in Yemen, which began in 2015 and initially involved a coalition of Arab states.
The Yemen Data Project recorded 25,054 Saudi-led coalition air raids between 2015 and 2022, according to figures cited in the letter. The organisations said extensive evidence showed that the air campaign attacked civilians and civilian infrastructure.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Gaza officials warn of imminent 'humanitarian catastrophe' as winter approaches
Gaza’s Government Media Office has accused Israel of violating its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire agreement, saying the continued violations have worsened the humanitarian crisis as the ceasefire approaches its first anniversary.
Israel had committed 5,147 violations that killed 1,421 Palestinians, injured 4,983 and caused the arrest of 198 people, the office said.
It also said 72,826 aid trucks had entered Gaza of an expected 210,600 under the agreement, while only 13,785 people had been allowed to travel in and out of the territory of an expected 35,000.
As winter approaches, the office warned of a “certain humanitarian catastrophe” as more than 1.5 million displaced Palestinians live in worn-out tents.
It said 162,000 of Gaza’s estimated 270,000 tents were already unusable and warned that more than 255 damaged buildings were in danger of collapse.
The office appealed to the international community and the UN agencies to intervene urgently, fully open Gaza’s crossings, facilitate medical evacuations and allow winter relief supplies into the territory.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Vance describes Iran’s leadership as ‘very confused’, says deal possible
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
Vance describes Iran’s leadership as ‘very confused’, says deal possible
US Vice President JD Vance said there is still scope for a deal with Iran if its leaders honour their commitments to Washington, while describing Tehran’s political decision-making system as “very confused”.
In an interview with journalist Vince Coglianese, Vance said President Donald Trump had made clear that “there is a universe where we can strike a deal with Iran, but that requires the Iranians to behave”.
He said Washington’s approach would be based on Iranian actions rather than statements.
Vance said Iran’s leadership involved “a number of different constituencies”, including hardliners, conservatives, moderates and clerics.
He also said Iran’s new supreme leader was “very detached” and not involved in day-to-day decision-making or public discussions about negotiations.

data.title: Middle East Eye: UKMTO reports strike on vessel in Strait of Hormuz
data.author: Qazi Zaid
data.summary:
UKMTO reports strike on vessel in Strait of Hormuz
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday that a vessel was hit by an apparent projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Monday evening, causing a fire.
The fire was later put out and the crew were all safe, with the vessel continuing its journey.
There was no reported environmental impact, and the extent of damage to the vessel was still being assessed, the UKMTO said.
The attack comes as attacks continue around the strategic waterway, disrupting global shipping and keeping the heat on oil markets.
